chief_complaint: sharp right upper quadrant abdominal pain after eating dinner
hpi_details: 6-hour history of steady, severe RUQ pain that began 1 hour after eating a fried chicken dinner. Pain radiates to the right shoulder blade. Associated with nausea and two episodes of bilious vomiting. Subjective fever at home. No jaundice or dark urine.
ideas: thinks she might have severe food poisoning from the dinner
concerns: worried because the pain is getting sharper when she takes a deep breath
expectations: wants strong pain relief and an ultrasound to see what is happening
pmh: obesity (BMI 32), hypercholesterolaemia, type 2 diabetes controlled with diet
social_hx: non-smoker, drinks wine socially on weekends, works as an accountant

investigation_events.title: STAT acute cholecystitis workup
investigation_events.availability_message: The STAT laboratory and right-upper-quadrant ultrasound results are now available; analgesia, fluids, and surgical consultation should not be delayed.

results.value: Multiple gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening to 5 mm, trace pericholecystic fluid, and a positive sonographic Murphy sign; common bile duct 5 mm

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Cholecystitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes keeping the patient NPO, IV fluid resuscitation, IV analgesia and antiemetics, and empiric IV antibiotics (e.g., co-amoxiclav), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sharp right upper quadrant abdominal pain after eating dinner

Key HPI features: 6-hour history of steady, severe RUQ pain that began 1 hour after eating a fried chicken dinner. Pain radiates to the right shoulder blade. Associated with nausea and two episodes of bilious vomiting. Subjective fever at home. No jaundice or dark urine.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals needed (check for pyrexia/tachycardia). Abdominal exam for RUQ tenderness and Murphy's sign. Bloods: FBC (WBC), CRP, LFTs (lipase/amylase to exclude pancreatitis), abdominal ultrasound.
Relevant background/PMH: obesity (BMI 32), hypercholesterolaemia, type 2 diabetes controlled with diet
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Cholecystitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Biliary colic without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever with right-upper-quadrant pain — suggests progression beyond simple biliary colic.
management_principles: Keep NPO, IV fluid resuscitation, IV analgesia and antiemetics, empiric IV antibiotics (e.g., co-amoxiclav), urgent RUQ ultrasound, surgical consultation for laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) Clinical Guidelines

reference_soap.subjective: 52F presenting with 6-hr severe RUQ pain radiating to right scapula postprandial (fatty meal). Nausea and vomiting x2. Positive inspiratory arrest (Murphy's sign history). No jaundice.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals needed (check for pyrexia/tachycardia). Abdominal exam for RUQ tenderness and Murphy's sign. Bloods: FBC (WBC), CRP, LFTs (lipase/amylase to exclude pancreatitis), abdominal ultrasound.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute cholecystitis secondary to cholelithiasis. DDx: biliary colic, acute pancreatitis, peptic ulcer perforation, right lower lobe pneumonia.
reference_soap.plan: Keep NPO, IV fluid resuscitation, IV analgesia and antiemetics, empiric IV antibiotics (e.g., co-amoxiclav), urgent RUQ ultrasound, surgical consultation for laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

learning_objectives: Elicit classical biliary pain characteristics including radiation to scapula and postprandial onset
Identify risk factors for gallstone disease (female, fertile/fifties, fat)
Differentiate acute cholecystitis from uncomplicated biliary colic by duration and systemic signs
Explain NPO status and need for surgical evaluation clearly

teaching.one_liner: Gallstones block the cystic duct and the gallbladder becomes inflamed, causing steady right-upper-quadrant pain after fatty meals, often with fever.
red_flags: Fever with right-upper-quadrant pain — suggests progression beyond simple biliary colic

must_ask.say: Did the pain start after eating a fatty or fried meal?
Has this pain lasted for hours, rather than easing off after a few minutes?

must_ask.objective: Radiation to the shoulder or back
must_ask.say: Does the pain spread to your shoulder blade or your back?
Have you had a fever or chills with this?
Have you felt sick or vomited?
Have you noticed your skin or eyes turning yellow, or your urine going dark?
Does it hurt more when you take a deep breath in?
